issues.title: Core MCP Server Setup and Communication
issues.objective: Establish the foundational Model Context Protocol (MCP) server structure in Go, enabling standard input/output (stdio) and HTTP/Server-Sent Events (SSE) communication.
issues.problem: The 'modex' project requires a robust, Go-native MCP server as its core platform to host all subsequent tools and interact with Large Language Models (LLMs). This foundational setup must correctly integrate the official Go SDK and support specified communication protocols.
changes: Initialize a new Go module (`go mod init modex-mcp-server`).
Integrate the `github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk` for MCP server implementation.
Implement basic server logic to support communication over stdio.
Implement basic server logic to support communication over HTTP/SSE.
issues.verification: Confirm that the server can start, receive basic MCP requests via stdio and HTTP/SSE, and respond appropriately.
out_of_scope: Implementation of specific MCP tools (e.g., diagnostics, search_docs).
Advanced error handling beyond basic server operations.
acceptance_criteria: A Go module named 'modex-mcp-server' is created.
The `go-sdk` is correctly imported and utilized.
The server can be run and accept connections via stdio.
The server can be run and accept connections via HTTP/SSE.

new_tests: Write unit tests for the server initialization and shutdown procedures, verifying graceful startup and termination.
Develop integration tests that simulate stdio and HTTP/SSE client connections, sending minimal valid MCP messages and asserting correct server responses.
Verify error handling for malformed requests or connection issues.
testing_strategy.test_patterns: Standard Go testing conventions using `*_test.go` files and `go test`.

risks: Potential compatibility issues with `go-sdk` if not used idiomatically.
Complexity in correctly implementing both stdio and HTTP/SSE transport layers.
issues.notes: Refer to `mcp-go` and `mcp-filesystem-server` for Go MCP server architecture examples.

issues.title: Documentation Indexing with SQLite FTS5
issues.objective: Implement a full-text search (FTS5) index using SQLite for comprehensive Go documentation, covering both the standard library and project dependencies.
issues.problem: Large Language Models often suffer from 'version skew' and 'dependency hallucination' when generating Go code. Providing a version-aware, indexed documentation source is crucial to mitigate these issues and ensure LLMs produce accurate and up-to-date code.
changes: Set up an SQLite database within the project.
Enable the FTS5 extension for the SQLite database.
Develop a Go module to crawl Go standard library documentation using `go doc`.
Develop a Go module to crawl documentation for project dependencies by inspecting `go.mod` and utilizing `go doc`.
Populate the FTS5 index with the collected documentation, ensuring version awareness.
issues.verification: Confirm that documentation for various Go versions and project dependencies is correctly indexed and searchable via FTS5.
out_of_scope: Implementation of the `search_docs` MCP tool (covered in MODEX-003).
Real-time synchronization or complex update strategies for the index (initial focus on building the index).
acceptance_criteria: An SQLite database file is created and accessible.
The FTS5 extension is active and usable.
Standard library documentation is successfully indexed.
Documentation for at least one external Go module dependency is successfully indexed.
Basic FTS5 queries on the index return relevant documentation entries.

new_tests: Write unit tests to verify the parsing of `go doc` output and extraction of relevant text for indexing.
Develop integration tests to ensure that the SQLite database is correctly initialized with FTS5 and that the indexing process populates the table with expected data.
Create tests to validate that FTS5 queries (e.g., `SELECT * FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH 'WaitGroup'`) return accurate results.
testing_strategy.test_patterns: Standard Go testing conventions using `*_test.go` files and `go test`.

research_questions: What is the most efficient way to extract and normalize text from `go doc` output for FTS5 indexing?
How can we ensure version awareness when indexing documentation for multiple Go versions or different versions of the same dependency?
risks: Performance bottlenecks during documentation crawling and indexing for large projects.
Challenges in accurately parsing and structuring documentation from diverse sources.
issues.notes: Engram and go-doc-bundler provide excellent examples of FTS5 integration and documentation crawling.

references.title: engram: Persistent memory system for AI coding agents. Agent-agnostic Go binary with SQLite + FTS5, MCP server, HTTP API, CLI, and TUI.
references.why: Highly relevant for demonstrating a complete implementation of a persistent memory system for AI agents using SQLite with FTS5 and an MCP server.

references.title: go-doc-bundler: A Go utility that crawls documentation websites and packages them into an offline bundle with full-text search capabilities.
references.why: Directly addresses the need to crawl and bundle documentation with full-text search, informing the FTS5 index implementation.

issues.title: MCP Tool: `get_diagnostics` (Orchestrator for all Diagnostics)
issues.objective: Develop a central `get_diagnostics` MCP tool that orchestrates and consolidates results from all specific diagnostic tools, providing a unified entry point for LLMs.
issues.problem: To effectively address various Go code issues (compilation, outdated dependencies, security, modernization, version skew), LLMs need a single, coherent diagnostic report. The `get_diagnostics` orchestrator will fulfill this by calling and aggregating results from individual diagnostic tools, including `get_go_version_info` as per feedback.
changes: Define the `get_diagnostics` MCP tool interface, accepting parameters relevant for comprehensive diagnostics (e.g., project path, specific checks to run).

Implement the orchestrator logic within `get_diagnostics` to sequentially or concurrently call the following specific diagnostic tools: `get_build_diagnostics`, `get_outdated_diagnostics`, `get_security_diagnostics`, `get_modernize_diagnostics`, and `get_go_version_info`.
Define a unified, structured output format for aggregated diagnostic results, making it easy for LLMs to parse and act upon.
Implement error handling and result merging for the aggregated diagnostic reports.
issues.verification: Confirm that `get_diagnostics` successfully invokes all sub-diagnostic tools, aggregates their results into a single, coherent report, and returns it in the defined format.
out_of_scope: Implementation details of the individual diagnostic tools (covered in MODEX-005, -006, -007, -008, -009).
Deep analysis of individual diagnostic findings (focus on orchestration).
acceptance_criteria: The `get_diagnostics` MCP tool is registered and discoverable.
A request to `get_diagnostics` successfully triggers calls to all specified sub-diagnostic tools.
All diagnostic results are merged into a single, structured JSON output.
The `get_go_version_info` results are included in the aggregated output.

new_tests: Write unit tests for the `get_diagnostics` handler, mocking the calls to sub-diagnostic tools to ensure correct orchestration and result aggregation.
Develop integration tests that call `get_diagnostics` on a sample Go project, verifying that the output contains expected results from each diagnostic category.
Test scenarios where some sub-diagnostic tools might fail or return no results, ensuring graceful handling by the orchestrator.
testing_strategy.test_patterns: Standard Go testing conventions using `*_test.go` files and `go test`.

research_questions: What is the most effective unified data structure for representing diverse diagnostic information for LLMs?
Should sub-diagnostic tools run concurrently or sequentially, and what are the performance implications?
risks: Complexity in defining a flexible and comprehensive unified output schema.
Potential for performance degradation if orchestration is not optimized.
issues.notes: The feedback explicitly mandates including `get_go_version_info` as a diagnostic tool orchestrated by `get_diagnostics`.

Integrate with `gopls` (or similar language server capabilities) to capture compilation errors and warnings.

issues.title: Prompt Development: `coding_modern_go` (Go 1.25+ Best Practices)
issues.objective: Develop comprehensive content for the `coding_modern_go` prompt to guide LLMs on generating modern, idiomatic Go 1.25+ code, addressing common failure modes.
issues.problem: LLMs often generate Go code with stale idioms, concurrency bugs, version skew, dependency hallucination, and general non-idiomatic patterns. A well-crafted, detailed prompt is essential to steer LLMs towards generating high-quality, up-to-date Go code that adheres to best practices and avoids common pitfalls.
changes: Draft detailed prompt content covering new features and changes introduced in Go 1.25 and 1.26.
Include guidelines on modern Go idioms, common design patterns (e.g., error handling, concurrency with channels and `context.Context`), and recommended standard library packages.

Provide explicit instructions to mitigate known LLM failure modes: emphasize correct `WaitGroup` usage to avoid deadlocks/leaks, advise against hallucinating non-existent dependencies, and guide towards current API usage.
Incorporate best practices for testing Go code, including table-driven tests and mock interfaces.
Structure the prompt for clarity and effectiveness when used by an LLM.
issues.verification: The prompt content is comprehensive, accurate, and clearly communicates modern Go best practices and LLM-specific guidance.
out_of_scope: Technical implementation of how this prompt is injected or managed by the MCP server.
Empirical testing of the prompt with LLMs (this is a content creation task).
acceptance_criteria: The prompt content clearly outlines Go 1.25/1.26 features.
It provides actionable advice for generating idiomatic Go code.
Specific instructions are included to prevent LLM concurrency bugs (e.g., WaitGroup misuse).
Guidance on avoiding dependency hallucination and version skew is present.
The prompt is well-structured and easy to understand for an AI agent.

new_tests: Manual review by Go experts to ensure technical accuracy and idiomatic correctness.
Internal dogfooding with LLMs (not part of this issue's scope, but the eventual verification method for the prompt's effectiveness).
testing_strategy.test_patterns: N/A, this is a content-based task rather than code implementation.

research_questions: What are the most effective prompting techniques to consistently elicit modern and idiomatic Go code from LLMs?
How granular should the prompt be in explaining Go language features versus expecting prior knowledge from the LLM?
risks: Prompt content quickly becoming outdated with new Go releases.
Difficulty in covering all possible LLM failure modes in a single prompt.
LLMs potentially 'overfitting' to the prompt, leading to less creative solutions.
issues.notes: Draw heavily from official Go documentation, style guides, and community best practices. Emphasize the 'why' behind certain Go patterns.

assumptions: The Go SDK for MCP (`github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk`) will provide stable and well-documented APIs for server implementation.
The `go doc` command provides sufficient information to build a comprehensive documentation index for FTS5.
Existing Go tooling (`go vet`, `go list`, `gopls`, `govulncheck`, `go fix`) can be programmatically invoked and their outputs reliably parsed.
The primary client for the MCP server will be an LLM, and the diagnostic and documentation outputs should be optimized for machine readability and actionability.
open_questions: What is the optimal strategy for managing the lifecycle and updates of the FTS5 documentation index (e.g., on-demand, scheduled, triggered by `go.mod` changes)?
How will version information be passed to and managed by the MCP server and its tools to ensure truly version-aware diagnostics and documentation searches?

Should MODEX provide specific recommendations for handling errors (e.g., `pkg/errors` vs. standard errors) or leave such stylistic choices to the LLM/user?
